The Persistence of Small Joys

There is a particular shade of light that appears only in late October, when the afternoon sun has begun its early descent but hasn't yet surrendered to the melancholy of winter. It filters through leaves that have turned but not yet fallen, casting everything in amber and gold, and for a few perfect minutes, the world seems to exist in a state of suspended grace. I have been thinking about this light lately, about how it arrives without announcement and departs without farewell, and about what it means to notice something so transient, so utterly uninterested in our attention.

We live in an age of documentation, of capture and curation, and I wonder sometimes if we are losing the art of unrecorded observation. The October light demands nothing. It does not improve your social media presence or provide material for cocktail party conversation. It simply exists, and in its existence, it offers a kind of relationship that is increasingly rare: one without exchange value, without leverage or utility. You can stand in that light and be changed by it, and no one will ever know. The change is real nonetheless.

I have been reading about mycelial networks, the vast underground fungal systems that connect trees in forests across the world. Through these networks, nutrients flow from established trees to seedlings struggling in shade, from dying trees to their thriving neighbors. The forest operates, in some sense, as a collective intelligence, a shared economy of sustenance that recognizes no individual ownership. Scientists call this the "wood wide web," which is charming in its nerdy way, but I find myself drawn to something beyond the science—the image of trees in silent conversation, of resources moving toward need without negotiation, without debt or expectation of return.

This is not how we have built our human world. We have built it on transaction, on the careful accounting of give and get, on contracts explicit and implicit. I am not naive enough to think this can simply be replaced with forest wisdom. We are not trees, and our complexity demands different arrangements. But I wonder what we have lost in our relentless balancing of accounts, our insistence that every gift carry obligation, every kindness be reciprocated, every moment of beauty be captured and converted to something else.

There is a café I visit sometimes, not because the coffee is exceptional but because an old man comes there every Tuesday and Thursday to play chess against himself. He sets up the board with careful precision, plays both sides with equal deliberation, and seems to exist in a state of complete absorption. I have never spoken to him. I do not know his name or his history. But watching him, I feel something I can only describe as relief—the relief of witnessing a person who has found a private language, a practice that makes sense to him alone, that requires no audience, no validation, no participation beyond his own divided attention.

Once, I saw him pause in the middle of a game, his hand hovering over a knight, and he smiled. It was not a performance of pleasure, not the social smile we deploy to reassure others. It was the smile of a man alone with a problem he had set himself, discovering something he had not expected. I wanted to know what he had seen, what move had pleased him, but wanting to know was different from needing to know. I let him keep it. This, too, feels like a practice I am trying to learn: the generosity of not asking, of allowing others their unshared experiences.

The philosopher Simone Weil wrote that attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity. She was thinking partly of religious attention, of the complete presence that prayer requires, but I think her insight extends further. To attend to something is to give it the gift of your finite self, your unrepeatable minutes, without guarantee of reward. The October light will not thank you. The chess player will not acknowledge your observation. The mycelial network does not know you exist. And yet the attention matters, or perhaps more precisely, the attention transforms the one who gives it.

I have been trying to practice this attention more deliberately, to resist the pull of constant productivity and documentation. It is difficult. The habits of utility are deeply ingrained. I find myself reaching for my phone to photograph a moment of unexpected beauty, and I have to consciously choose instead to simply be present, to let the moment pass through me without residue, without proof. There is anxiety in this—the fear of losing, of forgetting, of having nothing to show. But there is also freedom, the freedom of experience that exists only in its happening, that owes nothing to past or future.

The small joys persist, I am learning, not because we seize them but because we allow them. They are not accumulated but encountered, not possessed but inhabited. The October light will come again, though I may not be there to see it. The chess player will continue his solitary games. The forest will exchange its silent nutrients. And somewhere, someone will stand in a patch of unexpected warmth, will feel something shift in their chest, will choose not to name it or capture it or use it for anything at all, and in that choice, in that pure unproductive attention, will find something like peace.

This is what I want to write about, what I want to remember: not the grand narratives of achievement and acquisition, but the quiet persistence of moments that ask nothing and give everything, that pass through our lives like light through leaves, illuminating without staying, changing us in ways we may never fully understand.
